newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Mideast time-out needed, Israeli official says.
newsitem.headline: Mideast time-out needed, Israeli official says.

text.p: An Israeli official said on Thursday that Israelis and Palestinians needed a few months to cool off after an explosion of violence.
The West Bank and Gaza Strip were largely quiet after a Washington peace summit but many voiced doubts the calm would continue.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said the future of the Middle East peace process depended on Israeli moves.

"It depends how the Israelis will deal. Especially we are insisting they implement accurately and honestly what has been agreed upon and what was signed," he said before leaving for Tunis after talks with Moroccan King Hassan.
The Islamic Resistance Movement Hamas urged Palestinians to head to "total confrontations" with Israeli forces and settlers after Friday prayers in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
The senior Israeli official, who returned with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from the summit, told reporters a "stabilisation period" was needed.
"(This is) so the two military structures can gain confidence to work together," said the official, who spoke on condition he not be identified. He said a period of about 90 days "sounds right".

Joint Israeli-Palestinian patrols, part of three years of U.S.-nurtured peace deals, have ground to a halt in the West Bank and Gaza Strip since 58 Arabs and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed in gunbattles and clashes last week.

Their barrels pointing from hilltops, Israeli tanks remained in positions overlooking Palestinian towns ahead of U.S.-brokered talks due to start on Sunday in Gaza on Israel's long-delayed troop redeployment from Hebron.
"If anyone dares (to provoke Israel) he will experience the fire power of Israel's armour," Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said on Israeli radio.
Israeli officials predicted it would take weeks to carry out the Hebron redeployment but refused to be pinned down to a date.

U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross, who will join the talks on Sunday at the Erez crossing between Israel and the Gaza Strip, was likened by an Israeli official to "training wheels" on a bicycle, sticking around "until everybody learns to ride their bicycles again."
The talks could be moved soon to another location where non-stop sessions could take place, officials said.
Israeli government spokesmen hailed as a success the White House meeting that brought Netanyahu and Arafat together for only the second time since the Israeli leader was elected in May.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said all sides had won at the two-day summit called by President Bill Clinton. He offered to visit the Middle East himself if it would help.
But Palestinian officials called the summit a failure.

"I think the violence may resume because the summit failed to wipe out the causes of the explosion," said Ayman Hassan, a Palestinian policeman in Gaza. "The general feeling after the failure of the summit is disappointment and helplessness."
Arafat failed to win a target date for the partial pullout from the West Bank town of Hebron agreed by the previous Labour-led government.

Netanyahu also refused to close the tunnel exit in Arab Jerusalem's Moslem Quarter that triggered the violence. He has accused Arafat of having incited last week's violence -- the worst Israeli-Palestinian bloodshed since a 1993 peace deal.
In Hebron, where Israeli gunfire killed an 11-year-old Arab boy on Wednesday, some 3,000 Palestinians demonstrated, burning pictures of Netanyahu and U.S. and Israeli flags.
Soldiers ran through the city beating Palestinians and overturning vegetable stalls.
A Jewish settlers' leader said he was ready for war, believing that Palestinians frustrated by the peace process could again take to the streets.

Israeli defence officials were due to discuss soon with Netanyahu what to do about the tanks in the West Bank, Israeli officials said. They said Israel might ease the siege that bars Palestinian travel between autonomous cities, if calm prevailed.
